item.title: Shapla Chattar case: Prosecution files charges against Hasina, 40 others
item.description:
The prosecution has filed formal charges against ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina and 40 others in a crimes against humanity case over the killings during the Hefazat-e-Islam rally at Shapla Chattar in Dhaka's Motijheel in 2013.
Prosecutor Zahirul Amin submitted the formal charges to the registrar of the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) at around 10:45am on Monday. Prosecutor Marzina Raihan was also present.
A hearing in the case is scheduled to be held later in the day before a three-member bench of ICT-1 headed by Justice Md Golam Mortuza Majumder.
According to prosecution sources, the investigation report names 41 accused, including former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, former army chief General Aziz Ahmed, journalists Mozammel Babu and Farzana Rupa, and writer Shahriar Kabir.
On May 5, 2013, Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh staged a rally at Shapla Chattar in Dhaka's Motijheel, demanding implementation of its 13-point charter.
Following a day of tensions and clashes, members of the police, Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) carried out a joint overnight operation to clear the area.
Allegations that numerous people were killed during the operation later prompted an investigation by the International Crimes Tribunal into possible crimes against humanity.

item.title: FM attends Maldives Independence Parade
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman attended the Maldives' 61st Independence Day Parade in Malé as a special guest of the Maldivian government, reaffirming the close ties between the two South Asian nations.
The parade was held at Republic Square in Malé on Sunday, where Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam received Dr Rahman upon his arrival.
The event featured a ceremonial march-past and displays by different branches of the Maldives National Defence Force, showcasing the country's discipline, heritage and national pride as it celebrated the 61st anniversary of its independence.
Following the parade, Dr Rahman attended a cultural program highlighting the Maldives' rich traditions and cultural heritage. The day's celebrations concluded with a fireworks display.
Earlier, the foreign minister planted a Christina (Syzygium campanulatum) tree at Lonuziyaarai Park in Malé as part of the "Five Million Trees Project" launched by Maldivian President Dr Mohamed Muizzu.
Maldivian Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam and Climate Change, Environment and Energy Minister Ali Shareef attended the tree-planting ceremony.
Dr Rahman appreciated President Muizzu's initiative to expand the Maldives' green cover and highlighted Bangladesh's own ambitious afforestation programme.
He said the Bangladesh government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, is implementing an initiative to plant 250 million trees over the next five years.
The foreign minister said the initiatives undertaken by the leaders of the two countries reflected Bangladesh and the Maldives' shared commitment to environmental sustainability, climate action and safeguarding the planet for future generations.
Dr Rahman also recalled Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman's initiative to plant large groves of Azadirachta indica trees on the plains of Arafat in Saudi Arabia, which are popularly known as "Zia Trees".
Dr Rahman is visiting the Maldives at the invitation of the Maldivian government to join the country's 61st Independence Day celebrations as a special guest.

item.title: Flood-hit Chittagong Board HSC exams resume after 3-week suspension
item.description:
The Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations under the Chittagong Education Board resumed on Monday after being suspended for nearly three weeks due to floods and adverse weather conditions.
With the resumption, students under the board returned to examination halls for the first time since the suspension. Examinations also continued across the country's other nine general education boards, the Madrasa Education Board and the Technical Education Board as per the previously announced schedule.
According to the routine, examinations for Civics and Good Governance (First Paper), Biology (Theory, First Paper), and Business Organisation and Management (First Paper) began at 10am under the nine general education boards. The Food and Nutrition (First Paper) examination is scheduled for the afternoon.
Under the Madrasa Education Board, Alim examinees are sitting for Islamic History, Physics (Theory, Second Paper), and Tajweed (Second Paper for the Mujabbid Mahir stream). The Technical Education Board is holding the Human Resource Management-I examination for HSC (BMT) students.
On July 16, authorities suspended all remaining HSC and equivalent examinations under the Chittagong Education Board until further notice, citing the post-flood situation, the physical and mental condition of examinees, and disruption to road communications in affected areas.
The suspension also applied to the remaining Alim examinations under the Madrasa Education Board and HSC (BMT), HSC (Vocational), and Diploma in Commerce examinations under the Technical Education Board in the affected region.

item.title: 3 arrested over attempted rape on moving bus in Ashulia
item.description:
Police have arrested three people, including a bus driver and his assistant, over the attempted rape of a woman aboard a moving bus in Ashulia, Dhaka.
The arrestees are bus helper Md Musfequr Rahman Joni, 20, driver Md Imran, 35, and Imran's acquaintance, Md Suman Pramanik, 30.
According to Ashulia police, the woman and her acquaintance, Md Rubel, 27, boarded a Savar Paribahan bus at Gabtoli in Dhaka around 1:30am on Sunday, intending to travel to Nabinagar in Savar.
As the bus neared Nabinagar, after other passengers had disembarked, driver Imran allegedly handed over the steering wheel to helper Joni. Police said Imran then assaulted Rubel, threatened to kill him, and forced him off the bus. Imran also got off shortly afterwards, leaving the woman, Joni and Suman on board.
Police alleged that Joni, with Suman's assistance, then attempted to rape the woman inside the moving bus. The victim screamed for help.
After getting off the bus, Rubel called the national emergency service 999 and informed police.
Acting on the information, Ashulia police intercepted the bus at Rarapara bus stand by blocking its path with another vehicle. The woman was rescued, while Joni and Suman were arrested at the scene.
The victim later filed a case under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act.
Police subsequently arrested driver Imran during a raid in the Baraipara area of Ashulia around 3:30pm on Sunday.
Ashulia Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Tariqul Islam said police responded immediately after receiving the 999 call, rescued the victim and arrested the suspects.
He said all three accused have been arrested in connection with the case.

item.title: Hard drives stolen from 22 Education Ministry computers
item.description:
Hard drives and other computer components have allegedly been stolen from 22 computers at the Secondary and Higher Education Division under the Ministry of Education.
The division has filed a complaint with Shahbagh Police Station, alleging that an office assistant of the Public Works Department was involved in the theft after identifying him through CCTV footage.
The complaint was filed on Sunday by Md Abdur Rahim, administrative officer of the Secondary and Higher Education Division.
Confirming the matter, Shahbagh Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Moniruzzaman said police had received the complaint and were investigating.
According to the complaint, Md Mahbub Hossain, an office assistant of the Public Works Department, had access to keys for various rooms of the division's office.
He allegedly stole 22 computer hard drives, along with processors, RAM modules and printers, from different offices of the Secondary and Higher Education Division on June 14 and July 23.
The estimated value of the stolen items is Tk400,000.
The complaint also alleges that several other items, including cups and plates, went missing.
According to the complaint, CCTV footage captured the theft, and Mahbub was identified from the recordings.

item.title: Security guards vanish after Mirpur gold theft
item.description:
Around 259 bhori of gold jewellery was stolen from two jewellery shops at Shah Ali Shopping Complex in Mirpur, Dhaka, in the early hours of Sunday.
Police suspect the theft was carried out with the involvement of five market security guards, who have been missing since the incident.
According to Darus Salam police, the theft took place sometime between Saturday night and early Sunday.
The stolen jewellery belonged to Al Razzak Jewellers, owned by Jasim Uddin, and A Hossain Jewellers, owned by Abul Hossain, both located on the second floor of the shopping complex.
Darus Salam Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Dulal Hossain said preliminary findings suggest that around 200 bhori of gold ornaments were stolen from Al Razzak Jewellers and about 59 bhori from A Hossain Jewellers.
Describing it as a "well-planned theft," the OC said initial investigations indicate that the market's security guards were involved, along with three or four accomplices.
He said the guards had joined the market only a few days earlier with the intention of carrying out the theft.
Police also found that the national identity cards submitted by the guards during recruitment were fake, while their mobile phones have since been switched off.
The OC said police had obtained photographs of the suspects and were trying to identify them further by reviewing CCTV footage from the market.
According to investigators, security arrangements included both the market's own guards and a security guard assigned by the jewellery shops.
Police said the shop security guard was apparently rendered unconscious after being given sweets laced with a sedative.
CCTV footage also showed the market security guards allegedly taking part in the theft.
A case has been filed with Darus Salam Police Station. No arrests had been made as of 1am on Sunday.

item.title: Probe launched into 'poisoning' of water supply at Jungle Salimpur police outpost
item.description:
Police have launched an investigation after the water supply at the Alinagar Police Outpost in Chittagong's Jungle Salimpur was suspected to have been contaminated with poison or another toxic chemical substance.
The incident came to light on Sunday after three police personnel fell ill apparently after drinking water from the outpost.
Chittagong Superintendent of Police (SP) Md Masud Alam said personnel on duty noticed unusual foam and a strong stench in the water being used at the joint forces camp. Similar signs were later found in the camp's water tank, while an empty container believed to have contained a poisonous substance was recovered from the area.
"We cannot confirm yet whether it was poison, pesticide or any other chemical substance. The matter will be clear after receiving the laboratory report," he said.
Mohammad Mohinul Islam, Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Sitakunda Police Station, said three camp members noticed white foam while pouring water into a glass but did not initially consider it suspicious and drank the water. They later detected a strong chemical smell and soon fell ill.
The OC said the camp receives its drinking water through a pipeline connected to a nearby house.
Investigators suspect someone may have tampered with the supply line and mixed a chemical substance into the water.
Following the incident, water samples were collected and sent for laboratory testing, while the entire water tank was emptied and cleaned, he said, adding that the condition of the three affected police personnel is now stable and they are out of danger.
"The matter is under investigation," the OC said.
A temporary joint forces camp comprising personnel from the police, Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) has been established in the Salimpur jungle of Sitakunda, an area long regarded as a hideout for criminal and militant groups, to strengthen law and order.
On March 9, law enforcement agencies took control of the Salimpur jungle during a joint operation involving around 3,200 members of the Bangladesh Army, RAB, police and BGB.
Previous operations had failed to secure the area, with police and government officials coming under attack during earlier attempts.
On May 25, unidentified attackers targeted the joint forces camp under construction in the Alinagar area of Salimpur jungle, damaging it with an explosive device.
Later, a case was filed with Sitakunda Police Station over the incident, naming 242 people and accusing another 150 to 200 unidentified individuals.
However, the prime accused, Yasin, the alleged leader of the Yasin group, remains at large.

item.title: Growing hope
item.description:
In a country that has made remarkable progress in food production, a troubling reality still persists: Many children do not eat a sufficiently diverse and nutritious diet.
According to Unicef, nearly two-thirds of Bangladeshi children under five live in food poverty, consuming fewer than the minimum recommended food groups needed for healthy growth and development.
At the same time, malnutrition continues to undermine children's health, learning capacity, and future productivity.
Against this backdrop, the initiative known as the 48 Days Student Farmer is quietly demonstrating how a simple idea can address some of Bangladesh’s most pressing development challenges.
By transforming school grounds into learning gardens and students into young food producers, the initiative is cultivating far more than vegetables but rather is simultaneously nurturing knowledge, leadership, nutrition, and hope. Following a successful pilot in 20 schools involving around 1,700 students, this is being applied to approximately 864 schools nationwide.
The concept is refreshingly simple. Over a period of 48 days, students participate in guided gardening activities within their school premises. They learn how to prepare soil, sow seeds, care for plants, and harvest vegetables. Yet the real harvest extends far beyond the crops they grow.
For many children, nutrition is often discussed only in textbooks. Through school gardening, they experience it firsthand.
They learn where food comes from, why vegetables matter for health, and how climate-smart agricultural practices can help communities adapt to environmental challenges. Learning becomes practical, enjoyable, and relevant to everyday life.
What makes the initiative particularly powerful is that its impact does not stop at the school gate.
Students carry their new knowledge home. Many establish small homestead gardens with the support of their families, turning unused spaces into productive plots.
Parents become engaged, household food consumption improves, and communities begin to recognize the value of growing nutritious food close to home.
This ripple effect is especially significant for Bangladesh, where dietary diversity remains a challenge for many families.
When children become agents of change within their households, development gains become more sustainable. A school garden may occupy only a few square metres, but its influence can reach entire communities.
Its contribution to zero hunger and zero malnutrition is direct. By increasing access to fresh vegetables and promoting healthy eating habits, it strengthens household nutrition and food security.
Children are no longer passive beneficiaries; they become active participants in improving their own well-being.
Its contribution to education is equally important. Schools become more engaging when learning moves beyond memorization.
Students who participate in practical activities often develop a stronger connection to school, which can contribute to reducing dropout risks. A child who feels valued, involved, and inspired is more likely to stay in the classroom.
The initiative also helps build protective environments for children. By strengthening education, life skills, and awareness of child rights, it contributes indirectly to reducing vulnerabilities associated with child labour and child marriage.
When children remain engaged in school and envision brighter futures, the likelihood of exploitation diminishes.
Perhaps the most remarkable outcome, however, is the emergence of young leaders.
Students learn teamwork, problem-solving, communication, and responsibility. Many participate in school committees, support community activities, and encourage better nutrition and environmental practices among their peers and families.
In a world increasingly shaped by climate uncertainty, these leadership skills are invaluable. Today’s student gardeners are developing the confidence and practical knowledge needed to become tomorrow’s community leaders.
The success of the initiative also highlights the importance of partnerships.
Teachers, school management committees, parents, local government representatives, and agricultural extension officers all play critical roles.
Such collaboration ensures that the program is not perceived as an isolated project but rather as a shared community effort.
Of course, challenges remain. Climate shocks, excessive rainfall, droughts, and school holidays can affect garden maintenance.
Scaling a successful pilot to hundreds of schools also requires strong monitoring, quality training, and sustained community engagement.
Yet these challenges are not reasons for hesitation; they are opportunities for innovation.
Experiences from the program already demonstrate how communities can adapt through climate-smart techniques such as sack gardening, improved irrigation, and home-based cultivation.
The significance of this initiative lies not only in what it produces, but in what it represents. It reminds us that some of the most effective solutions are often the simplest.
A seed planted by a child can grow into a vegetable. But it can also grow into knowledge, confidence, resilience, and social change.
As Bangladesh continues its development journey, investments in children must remain at the centre of our efforts.
School gardens may not solve hunger and malnutrition on their own, but they offer a practical, affordable, and scalable pathway toward healthier communities and more resilient futures.
Sometimes, national transformation begins not with grand infrastructure or sophisticated technology, but with a handful of seeds, a patch of soil, and a child willing to learn.
If nurtured carefully, the 48 Days Student Farmer initiative could become one of Bangladesh’s most inspiring examples of how small actions can yield extraordinary results.
Mohammad Ruhul Amin is the technical manager -- livelihood of World Vision Bangladesh.

item.title: When public data becomes a fraudster's paradise
item.description:
The caller on the other end spoke with the crisp, measured cadence of a senior bureaucrat.
He introduced himself as a "deputy secretary" from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.
Had he offered general pleasantries or vague institutional jargon, I would have ended the call within seconds. But he didn’t.
Instead, he casually reeled off specifics that made me pause: The exact month two years ago when my son was enlisted as a performer at Bangladesh Betar, followed by the precise details of his recent artist grade upgrade.
Every detail was spot-on.
The punchline arrived with bureaucratic smooth-talking.
To "disburse" the back-pay and revised remuneration tied to his upgraded grade, the ministry needed to verify a few financial credentials.
All I had to do was provide my bank account details and debit card number over the phone.
I knew it was a scam. The caller was blocked shortly after, though I allowed the conversation to linger just long enough to see how far he would push, how far he would go to coerce those sensitive financial digits out of me.
But as I hung up, a far more troubling question lingered in the air: How on earth did a telephone scammer acquire a granular, internal ledger of my son’s bureaucratic record from a state-run broadcasting institution?
My experience, it turns out, was far from an isolated glitch.
It is a symptom of a systemic disease quietly metastasizing across Bangladesh’s public sector: The alarming, unvetted leakage of private data from institutions where citizens are required to hand over their most intimate details.
The anatomy of an institutional breach
Consider the unsettling reality currently unfolding at Jahangirnagar University (JU).
Over the past six months, at least 66 students and their families have reported falling victim to organized, targeted fraud rings.
The tactics used by these syndicates are terrifyingly personal and engineered for maximum panic.
In one instance, the father of a postgraduate chemistry student in the university’s 48th batch received a late-night call from a man claiming to be an officer with the Detective Branch (DB) of police.
The caller claimed his son had been picked up in a drug sweep, accompanied by background sounds of a young man weeping.
The frantic father was ordered to immediately send money via mobile financial services to secure his son’s release.
He was already on his way to the local agent shop when family members managed to reach the student, safe in his residential hall.
In other cases, scammers posed as university faculty or staff from the registrar’s office.
Calling parents directly, they claimed that technical errors were blocking the transfer of government stipends or merit scholarships.
They asked for banking credentials and one-time passwords (OTPs) to "rectify" the issue. One family lost Tk36,000 in minutes; another lost Tk10,000.
What makes these attacks so devastating is not merely the cruelty of the extortion, but the uncanny precision of the information used to pull them off.
Callers knew the students’ full names, exact departments, academic years, residential halls, registration details, and -- crucially -- the private contact numbers of their parents.
Where did this data come from?
The victims themselves noted that the specific contact details used by the callers were the exact ones submitted on official admission forms years prior -- information that was never meant to be public.
Routine advisories for criminal negligence
When confronted with these incidents, institutional leadership almost reflexively defaults to deflection.
Officials at Jahangirnagar University suggested that scholarship lists published on public websites might be the source, or that fraudsters were simply guessing numbers at random.
Such explanations are completely detached from reality. Public award lists do not contain parents' personal mobile numbers or non-public admission records.
Random number generators do not magically pair a father's phone number with his child's specific academic batch and department at a state university.
The reality is far simpler and far more damaging: Personal databases maintained by public institutions are leaking like a sieve.
Whether through unauthorized employee access, third-party vendor compromise, poor digital hygiene, or outright internal collusion, confidential records are routinely finding their way into the hands of organized criminal rings.
Yet, the administrative response remains painfully predictable. Bureaucrats issue routine warning notices instructing students and parents to "exercise caution."
They promise to pass rogue phone numbers to the police and wash their hands of the matter.
This approach is fundamentally inadequate. Telling citizens to be vigilant while ignoring the wide-open back door through which their private data was stolen is institutional gaslighting.
When a public university or state ministry collects personal data, it incurs a legal and moral obligation to protect it.
Failing to safeguard that information is not an administrative oversight; it is criminal negligence.
Demanding accountability
We must stop treating data harvesting and financial scams as inevitable hazards of the digital age.
They are direct consequences of institutional failure.
When young applicants submit their personal histories to a university, or when artists register their details with a state broadcaster, they hand over those details in good faith.
They trust that the institution will act as a responsible custodian. When that trust is betrayed, the institution cannot simply stand by as a passive observer.
We need to start asking hard, uncomfortable questions:
Answering these questions requires far more than internal committee observations or surface-level public advisories.
It demands comprehensive, independent criminal investigations.
Cybercrime units must trace not only the extortionists at the end of the phone line, but also the origin point where the data leaked.
If administrative staff or system administrators failed to secure these records -- or worse, sold them -- they must be identified, prosecuted, and publicly held to account.
Until public institutions face real consequences for failing to protect the data entrusted to them, sensitive records will continue to circulate among fraudsters.
As long as official negligence goes unchecked, the bond of trust between citizens and the state will remain fundamentally broken.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: 'Red Ivory' mango draws interest in Chapainawabganj
item.description:
In Bangladesh’s famed mango-producing district of Chapainawabganj, a striking crimson fruit is turning heads and drawing curious visitors, offering a glimpse of how exotic varieties could diversify the country's mango industry.
Rows of "Red Ivory" mangoes now hang in clusters from trees in a two-bigha orchard at Basantapur village in Shibganj upazila, where farmer Kabir Ali has successfully cultivated the foreign variety, attracting growers, students and fruit enthusiasts from across the district.
Known primarily as a vegetable farmer, Kabir's journey into cultivating the exotic mango began during a visit to Gaibandha, where he first encountered the Red Ivory variety. Impressed by its vibrant red colour, large size and commercial potential, he decided to bring the variety to his hometown.
Two years ago, he collected 340 saplings and established the orchard beside his home at a cost of around Tk150,000.
The trees produced fruit for the first time last year, yielding about five mounds of mangoes, which he sold at Tk5,500 per mound.
This season, however, nearly every tree has borne fruit.
Large crimson mangoes now cover the orchard, and the fruits are expected to reach the market within the next few weeks.
"Last year the harvest was small, but I received a good price. This year the trees are heavily laden with fruit. If the market price remains favourable, I hope to recover my investment and earn a profit," Kabir told UNB.
The unusual appearance of the mangoes has transformed Kabir's orchard into an attraction, with visitors arriving daily to see the rare variety firsthand.
Sanaullah, a local college student, said he had previously seen Red Ivory mangoes only on YouTube.
"Now I can see and even taste them in my own area. It's a wonderful experience. The mango looks beautiful and tastes excellent as well," he said.
Ataur Rahman, a mango grower from Laughatta area of Shibganj, said he visited the orchard after hearing about the foreign variety.
"The fruits are surprisingly large. Each mango appears to weigh between 800 grams and over one kilogram. The market value also seems promising. Seeing the orchard has inspired me to cultivate this variety next year," he said.
Another visitor, Robiul Islam from Chapainawabganj town, said he had also seen videos of the variety online but wanted to experience it in person.
"I am truly impressed after seeing the orchard with my own eyes," he said.
Habibur Rahman, who has been caring for the orchard since its establishment, said consumer response to the fruit was encouraging from the very beginning.
"When we harvested the first batch last year and took it to Kansat market, the mangoes sold out within a very short time," he said.
"We received a good price, and there was strong demand. This year almost every tree has produced fruit. We are hopeful of another successful season."
He added that people visit the orchard almost every day to learn more about the variety.
Deputy Director of the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) in Chapainawabganj, Md Atikul Islam, said the district is home to more than 300 mango varieties, with growers increasingly showing interest in introducing foreign cultivars.
"The DAE is providing technical support and guidance to farmers who want to cultivate new varieties," he said.
According to the official, Red Ivory is a late-season variety, allowing growers to market the fruit after the peak mango season when supplies are lower and prices are generally higher.
He expressed optimism that Kabir Ali would benefit financially from this year's harvest
The success of Red Ivory cultivation is being seen as more than an individual achievement.
Local farmers and agricultural officials believe the variety could open new opportunities for Bangladesh's mango sector by extending the marketing season and introducing a premium fruit with strong consumer appeal.
If proper orchard management and marketing systems can be ensured, they say, the vivid red mango could emerge as a profitable addition to the country's expanding fruit industry while encouraging more growers to experiment with high-value exotic varieties.

item.title: Dhaka air quality remains moderate Monday morning
item.description:
Dhaka's air quality remained moderate on Monday morning, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 79.
The capital ranked 18th among the world's most polluted cities at 8:10 am, according to the AQI scale, while its air quality was classified as "moderate."
Pakistan’s Lahore, Uganda's Kampala and Indonesia’s Jakarta occupied the first three spots on the list with AQI scores of 195, 179 and 177, respectively.
An AQI between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate" with an acceptable air quality while AQI between 101 and 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as ‘unhealthy’. AQI readings between 201 and 300 are termed ‘very unhealthy’, and anything above 301 is considered ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI is a daily indicator of air quality, showing how clean or polluted the air is and the possible health effects people may experience.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with severe air pollution. Air quality usually worsens during winter and improves in the monsoon season.
According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic respiratory diseases, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Japan's beloved monkey Punch turns one, receives thousands of birthday wishes
item.description:
Punch, the orphaned monkey at a Japanese zoo who won hearts around the world by cuddling an orangutan plush toy, is celebrating his first birthday on Sunday with thousands of birthday messages from admirers.
Although Punch no longer carries the toy and now happily plays with other monkeys, he remains one of the biggest attractions at the Ichikawa City Zoological and Botanical Garden.
Punch was abandoned by his mother shortly after birth a year ago, likely because she was exhausted. Zoo keepers hand-raised him and gave him a stuffed orangutan to help him develop the gripping skills newborn macaques need to survive.
Now fully grown into an active young monkey, Punch blends in with about 50 other monkeys in the enclosure. Still, visitors continue to flock to see him.
According to zoo director Takashi Yasunaga, Punch has received around 2,500 birthday cards and messages from supporters in Japan and abroad. Many of them are displayed at a special birthday exhibition inside the zoo, where visitors can also watch videos showing Punch's journey from his first days.
Yasunaga said the past year had been unforgettable for the zoo staff, recalling how two keepers devoted themselves to caring for Punch during the hot summer when he was born.
After six months of special care, Punch joined the monkey enclosure in January. Adjusting to life with the other monkeys was not easy, but it was during this period that he became an internet sensation.
In February, photos of Punch hugging his plush toy after being pushed away by other monkeys went viral on social media, attracting tens of thousands of visitors to the zoo, about half of them from overseas.
Supporters rallied behind him using the hashtag #HangInTherePunch, inspired not only by his adorable appearance but also by his determination to earn acceptance from the other monkeys.
Among those visiting the birthday exhibition was Kumi Ishizawa from Kobe, who said she first discovered Punch on social media while recovering from an illness.
"He inspired me," she said. "I kept telling myself I would get better and come to see Punch. Now I've finally made it, and I'm so happy."
Another fan, Yeye Lights, who has lived in Ichikawa for years, said she had never visited the zoo until her daughter in the Philippines introduced her to Punch online.
She has since become a regular visitor and even bought an annual pass.
"I have a cake for Punch-kun and I'm celebrating with my friends," she said, while thanking the two keepers who raised the young monkey.

item.title: Bangladesh excited for next tours as Joty sets lofty goal
item.description:
Bangladesh captain Nigar Sultana Joty is already looking forward to upcoming tours of Australia, New Zealand and England as the team readies their focus to the upcoming Asian Games in Japan.
The Asian side have white-ball tours to Australia and New Zealand awaiting them later in the year and will travel to England in the middle of 2027 for another six fixtures against the ICC Women's T20 World Cup runners up.
While Bangladesh will face a task in those matches, Joty is looking forward to the challenge and wants her teammates to rise to the occasion against three of the biggest teams in women's cricket.
“This is a very big opportunity for our team,” Joty said.
“We have always wanted to play in places like Australia, New Zealand or England because playing there helps develop your skills much more.
“Since we recently played in England and did well there, there is definitely a reflection of that.”
Those recent matches in England that Joty references came at the recent T20 World Cup, where Bangladesh managed two victories from five appearances to finish in fourth place in their group behind Australia, South Africa and Asian rivals India.
They may have to tackle India once again at the upcoming Asian Games in Japan, with Bangladesh scheduled to face China first-up at the eight-team tournament ahead of a potential final four matchup with Harmanpreet Kaur's side.
And while recent rain at home has made it tough for Bangladesh to prepare for the Asian Games that commences on September 17, Joty revealed she has high hopes for the side at the tournament and is aiming to at least reach the title decider.
“We want to prepare in a way that allows us to approach this Asia Cup better than we did last year,” she said.
“With the amount of rain currently affecting every venue in Bangladesh, we will still try to prepare in the best possible way before going there and definitely aim to play in the final.”

item.title: Japan's 'King Kazu', 59, scores his first goal for four years
item.description:
The 59-year-old former Japan striker Kazuyoshi Miura scored his first competitive goal in almost four years when his Fukushima United side strolled to a 7-0 win at the weekend.
In his 41st professional season, the grey-haired veteran nicknamed "King Kazu" netted Japan third division side Fukushima's fifth in an Emperor's Cup qualifier against Iwaki Furukawa FC, his first goal since November 2022.
Miura latched on to a 52nd-minute cross by Takatora Einaga inside the box to slot home, rolling back the years to beat two defenders to the ball.
"It was a bit of a scramble, but what matters is that we were in the right spots, so I think we positioned ourselves well," Miura said.
"I wanted to live up to the expectations of everyone, including the coach who gave me the opportunity to play until that point.
"Above all, I was so happy that, even when we were already way ahead, the players, staff, and fans were all able to celebrate that one goal together with such joy."
Miura made his professional debut in 1986 for Brazilian team Santos and has also played for teams in Italy, Croatia, Australia and Portugal.
He helped put football in Japan on the map when the professional J-League was launched in 1993.
He made his Japan debut in 1990 but was famously left out of the squad for their first World Cup finals appearance in 1998, despite scoring 55 goals in 89 games for the national side.
Miura signed for Fukushima United on loan in January and said he wanted to repay his new team's faith in him with goals and assists.
He spent last season with fourth-tier Atletico Suzuka, making eight goalless appearances as they were relegated to Japan's regional leagues.

item.title: 'Just cramp' - Lyles pulls up early in 200m US title bid
item.description:
US sprint star Noah Lyles pulled up with cramp in the 200m final at the US athletics championships on Sunday, his bid for a title double undone as Garrett Kaalund claimed the victory.
Lyles, who won the 100m on Friday in a world-leading 9.79sec, pulled up as he came off the turn and jogged to the line, telling reporters he felt a grabbing sensation in his right thigh.
"I'm like, yeah, there's no reason to keep pushing that," he said. "I just decided to cut it off."
Fans at Icahn Stadium in New York were stunned, but the 2024 100m Olympic gold medallist downplayed potential injury concerns.
"It's just cramp. I've got some electrolytes here, I'm going to chug them down. I'm going to rest."
Lyles walked over to give Kaalund a congratulatory hug after the 22-year-old captured the title in 20.04sec.
"It's kind of crazy," Kaalund said.
Brandon Hicklin was second and Maximilian Thomas third, both credited with a time of 20.29sec.
Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, a treble gold medallist at last September's world championships, won the women's 200m in 21.69sec -- just one-hundredth off her personal best.
Jefferson-Wooden came off the turn in front and powered home with Cambrea Sturgis second in 22.22 and Camryn Dickson third in 22.58.
Jefferson-Wooden had opted out of the 100m, which was won by Sha'Carri Richardson.
In a year with no world championships or Olympic team berths on the line, some well-known names opted out of the national championships or tweaked their programs, but there were still plenty of familiar winners.
Tara Davis-Woodhall pushed her long jump winning streak to 19 competitions in dramatic style, unleashing a leap of 7.16m on her sixth and final attempt to triumph.
Davis-Woodhall hasn't lost in the event since a runner-up finish at the 2023 world championships, a streak that includes 2024 Olympic gold and last year's world title.
Her final jump carried her past Alyssa Jones, who settled for second on 6.96, and Monae' Nichols, who took bronze in 6.92.
"Today I was like, 'Let's try to do one and done, please," Davis-Woodhall said. "And of course it never works out that way. It was a battle for sure."
- Close call -
Cordell Tinch, the 110m hurdles world champion, won his first national title by the narrowest of margins, edging Bradley Franklin by four one-thousandths of a second.
Both were credited with a time of 13.00sec, but when the times were expanded Tinch got the nod at 12.993 to Franklin's 12.997.
Tinch said he knew at the line he'd bagged the win.
"I knew when we crossed the line it didn't matter how close he was," he said. "I knew I took first."
Two-time reigning Olympic champion and last year's world champion Valarie Sion won her eighth straight women's discus title with a throw of 69.54m.
She held off Cierra Jackson, who took second at 67.40 just a week after topping Sion at the London Diamond League.
And Cooper Lutkenhaus, the 17-year-old sensation who won the indoor 800m world title and has bagged two Diamond League victories this year, won his first outdoor 800m national title in 1min 43.48sec.
Lutkenhaus made his move with 200m to go and pulled away for a crushing victory over Wes Ferguson, who clocked 1:44.55.
"It was amazing," said Lutkenhaus, who let out a mighty roar as he broke the tape to achieve his goal of winning both the indoor and outdoor US titles this year in his final race of the season.

item.title: Aussie great McEvoy masters Commonwealth gold
item.description:
Australian swimming great Cameron McEvoy blew away the field to win his first individual Commonwealth Games gold in the 50 metres freestyle as England's Adam Ramsay-Peaty bounced back to reach the final of the 50m breaststroke.
McEvoy smashed the Commonwealth Games record and led home an Aussie 1-2-3 from Flynn Southham and Jamie Jack.
The 32-year-old had previously won silver and bronze in the 50m freestyle back in Glasgow in 2014 and an home soil in the Gold Coast four years later.
The Olympic champion over 50m stormed out of the blocks to add a fourth Commonwealth gold to his three relay wins, obliterating the Games record in the process.
Ramsay-Peaty said he has a "battle plan" for Monday's 50m breaststroke final to ensure there is no repeat of his tears after finishing third in the 100m final.
The 31-year-old is aiming to become the first English swimmer to win gold at four different Commonwealth Games.
But he qualified just third fastest for the final behind 100m breaststroke champion Sam Williamson and South Africa's Michael Houlie.
"In sport, it's not really about when you get beat down because it's going to be inevitable," said Ramsay-Peaty.
"It's actually how long it takes you to look at it, respect it, and turn it around for tonight, and I'm really happy with that. I've got a great trajectory for tomorrow."
Lani Pallister secured her second gold of the meet with a dominant display to win the women's 1500m.
There was a shock in the women's 100m backstroke as 20-year-old Australian Iona Anderson edged out hot favourite Kylie Masse of Canada.
Australia also extended their clean sweep of the relays so far in the men's 4x200m freestyle.
But there was more variety on the top of the podium at the pool than in recent days as the Aussies did not have things all their own way.
South Africa's Pieter Coetze added gold in the 200m backstroke to his 50m gold on Saturday.
Canada's Josh Liendo edged out Australia's Matthew Temple by just one hundredth of a second to win the men's 100m butterfly.
And there was more joy for hosts Scotland as Angharad Evans produced a late fightback to win gold in the women's 100m breaststroke.
- Gymastics joy for Scotland, Canada -
Reuben Ward also struck gold for hosts in the men's gymnastics all-around final.
The 21-year-old held off a charge from Canada's Felix Dolci to secure gold by just 0.200 of a point with Australia's Jesse Moore in third.
"I knew I could do it, but to actually do it. When the score came through, it is just jubilation and joy," said Ward.
"Incredible! I'm so lucky to be in this position. I would've have been in this position without my family and my team-mates. It is like climbing a mountain."
Dolci, who was part of Canada's team gold, twice fell of the pommel horse on his opening apparatus before roaring back with five near flawless displays to nearly snatch victory.
"I wanted to show that it's never done until it's done. That's something I deeply value and I'm glad I was able to showcase that," said Dolci.
There was a Canadian gold in the women's all-around final as Ellie Black beat Breanna Scott of Australia and 16-year-old teammate Lia-Monica Fontaine.
"I'm so proud. My goal was not to come in and win. It was to come in and compete again," said 30-year-old Black. "To come out on top, is the cherry on top. I love the Commonwealths, it's so fun to be here."
In the biggest clash of the netball pool stages Australia produced a dominant 66-47 win over England.
New Zealand edged Jamaica 53-48 in the other big showdown of the day in Pool B.

item.title: India reclaim top T20I ranking after Zimbabwe success
item.description:
India are back to the No.1 position in the ICC Men's T20I Team rankings after taking an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series against Zimbabwe in Harare.
The current ICC Men's T20 World Cup champions regained the top spot from England, who had dethroned the Men in Blue post a 4-0 T20I series win at home.
The Indian batters took charge in the second T20I against Zimbabwe, after a dominating victory in the first T20I which was led by the bowlers and a record knock by Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
After losing two early wickets, Ishan Kishan and Shreyas Iyer came together to stitch a 66-run partnership, before Tilak Varma notched up a superb knock. (60 off 29 balls)
The highest scorer of the game, Kishan (81 off 44 balls) while speaking to the reporters post the match said, "We were down two wickets, but at the same time as a batter batting at no.3, your job is to just watch the ball and play your natural game."
"You also have to understand the wicket, there were a lot of thoughts going in whether we want to end up getting 250, 230 or if the wicket is just about getting 170-180 runs.
"Shreyas Iyer came in and we just wanted to build a partnership and take the innings deep. And I think we executed our plans in a good manner."
Chasing a tall target of 220, the Chevrons lost five wickets inside the first nine overs and were eventually bundled out for 129 as India took an unassailable lead in the T20I series.
The two teams will lock horns again on July 26, Sunday.

item.title: Nolan's 'The Odyssey' tops North American box office for 2nd week
item.description:
Christopher Nolan's latest blockbuster, "The Odyssey," retained the top spot at the North American box office in its second week, taking in an additional $87 million, industry estimates showed Sunday.
The film from Universal had an "outstanding hold" for its second weekend, industry analyst David A Gross said, after it dropped only about 30 percent from its $124 million debut.
"Once or twice a year a movie opens big and then plays for weeks and weeks... 'The Odyssey' is showing that kind of holding power, and Christopher Nolan has done it before," said Gross.
With an additional $353 million overseas, the film has already grossed $640 million worldwide.
Based on Homer's ancient epic poem, the star-studded film tracks hero Odysseus as he faces obstacle after obstacle on his way home from the Trojan War.
It is the first film ever to be shot entirely on IMAX film cameras, as Nolan leaned into filmmaking heritage for this modern adaption of one of humanity's oldest stories.
Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway lead the cast as Odysseus and Penelope, with Tom Holland portraying their son Telemachus.
Second place went to "Moana," Disney's latest live-action remake of one of its animated hits.
It took in an additional $10.5 million in its third week out, for a total domestic haul of $102 million and $125 million more overseas.
"Disney spent $250 million to reimagine the oceanic-set movie, so 'Moana' will struggle to swim to profitability in its theatrical run," commented Variety.
Third place also went to Disney and its fifth installment of the animated "Toy Story" franchise.
It took in $10 million in its sixth week, breaking the $1 billion-mark at the global box office.
It is the highest grossing film of the year so far, Variety reported.
Fourth place went to Bleecker Street's "Hadestown: The Musical," with $9.7 million.
The adaptation of the Tony-award-winning musical blends two ancient Greek myths with themes of love and class struggle, set in the Depression-era world.
Gross called the opening "very good for the genre."
Fifth place went Universal's "Minions & Monsters," with $9.6 million, for a total global haul of $381 million.
Round out the top 10 were:
"The Invite" ($2.64 million)
"Evil Dead Burn" ($2.61 million)
"Young Washington" ($2.0 million)
